title: Enhancing Primary Teacher Training through Academic Portfolios in Advanced Mathematics Courses
extended_summary:
This paper examines a persistent challenge in primary teacher education: the gap between advanced mathematical theory and the practical knowledge future primary teachers need for classroom instruction. The authors ask whether academic portfolios can serve as a purpose-driven assessment method that helps preservice teachers connect abstract mathematics content to teaching practice, while also improving engagement, assessment quality, and anxiety related to mathematics.

The intervention was implemented in two advanced mathematics courses, Algebra and Number Systems I and II, within the primary teacher education program at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile. The portfolio approach was introduced through a negotiated learning contract between instructors and teacher candidates, structured rubrics, reflective writing, draft-and-feedback cycles, presentations, and discussion tables. The participants were 37 female preservice teachers in their ninth and tenth semesters, all specializing in mathematics education and concurrently completing professional teaching practice.

Using attendance records, grade trends, platform analytics, self-assessments, peer evaluations, and reflective texts, the study reports increased attendance, stronger engagement, improved grades, and more positive perceptions of learning and organization. Participants also reported that portfolios helped them connect course content to teaching, support self-regulated learning, and reduce mathematics anxiety. The paper concludes that academic portfolios may be a useful way to strengthen mathematics teacher preparation, though the authors note that causal claims are limited by the study design and that more rigorous, larger-scale research is needed.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-site, mixed-methods, pre/post descriptive study with no control group or random assignment. It provides useful practice-based evidence, but the causal credibility is limited and outcomes rely partly on self-report and observational trends.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported improvements are promising but appear modest and are not supported by causal effect sizes. The study focuses on a small preservice teacher sample in one university setting, so generalizable impact is unclear.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports improved performance in two primary-teacher mathematics courses after introducing academic portfolios. In MAT2920, the average grade increased from 4.43 in the prior semester to 5.89 when portfolios were introduced, and later to 6.44; in MAT2925, grades rose from 5.52 to 5.80 and then 6.44. These are descriptive, uncontrolled semester-to-semester comparisons rather than causal estimates.
finding.measure: Course grades on the Chilean 1.0–7.0 scale in Algebra and Number Systems I and II

finding.finding_summary: Teacher candidates reported better engagement, increased intrinsic motivation, and reduced mathematics anxiety after portfolio implementation. On the end-of-semester survey, 11 of 12 respondents (91.7%) said alternative assessment methods such as portfolios helped mitigate math-anxiety-related feelings, and all participants reported strong time investment and positive alignment between effort and grades.
finding.measure: Self-assessment survey responses on motivation, engagement, and mathematics anxiety
finding.study_size: n=12 survey respondents for anxiety item; n=37 participants overall

finding.finding_summary: The portfolio process was associated with stronger self-regulation, time organization, reflection, and peer-evaluation skills. In self-reports, 100% of respondents said portfolios improved time organization and 85.7% reported gains in self-study; peer review and reflective paragraphs were used to support metacognitive engagement and critical assessment of classmates' work.
finding.measure: Self-assessment surveys, peer evaluation surveys, and reflective portfolio paragraphs
finding.study_size: n=37 overall; n=12 survey respondents for some items; n=7 peer-evaluation subgroup
